item.title: Put-Call Parity: Why a Call and a Put Are Tied Together
item.summary: Put-call parity says that for European options with the same strike, expiry and underlying, a call and a put cannot be priced independently, because certain combinations give identical payoffs. It lets you back out a missing option price and spot arbitrage.

sections.heading: The intuition: two routes to the same destination
sections.body_markdown:
Think of two travel routes that always arrive at the same place at the same time. They must cost the same, or everyone would book only the cheaper one.

In options, a **call** is the right to buy the underlying at a fixed **strike** $X$ on the expiry date. A **put** is the right to sell at $X$. A **European** option can only be exercised at expiry, not earlier. Put-call parity comes from building two portfolios that end up with the same value at expiry.

sections.heading: The two portfolios
sections.body_markdown:
**Fiduciary call** = a European call + a risk-free zero-coupon bond that pays exactly $X$ at expiry. The bond costs $X/(1+r)^T$ today, where $r$ is the annual risk-free rate and $T$ is the time to expiry in years.

**Protective put** = a European put + one share of the underlying. The put sets a floor under the share.

At expiry, with the share worth $S_T$:
- If $S_T > X$, the call is exercised. The fiduciary call is worth $(S_T - X) + X = S_T$. The put expires worthless, so the protective put is worth $S_T$.
- If $S_T \le X$, the call expires worthless and the bond pays $X$. The put pays $X - S_T$, and with the share the protective put is worth $X$.

Both portfolios are worth $\max(S_T, X)$ in every outcome.

sections.heading: From equal payoffs to equal prices
sections.body_markdown:
Identical payoffs at expiry force identical costs today, otherwise there is a risk-free profit (an **arbitrage**). Using $c_0$ and $p_0$ for today's call and put prices and $S_0$ for the spot price:

$$c_0 + \frac{X}{(1+r)^T} = p_0 + S_0$$

The parity must hold with the **same strike, same expiry and same underlying** for the call and the put. If you know three of the four items (call, put, spot, PV of strike), you can solve for the fourth. Rearranging gives $p_0 = c_0 - S_0 + X/(1+r)^T$.

This version assumes the underlying pays no income during the option's life. Adjustments for cash flows and the forward-based form belong to the next learning objective.

sections.heading: Rearranging: synthetic positions and arbitrage
sections.body_markdown:
Moving terms around shows that each instrument can be rebuilt from the others:
- **Long call** = long put + long stock + borrow $X/(1+r)^T$ (short the bond).
- **Long put** = long call + short stock + buy the bond with face $X$.
- **Long call, short put** has the payoff $S_T - X$, like a forward-style purchase at $X$.

If the two sides of the parity equation differ, sell the expensive portfolio, buy the cheap one, and pocket the difference today with no risk at expiry.

**Why only European?** An American option can be exercised early, so the two portfolios need not match at every date. The exact equality is a European-option result.

worked_example.problem: A European call on a non-dividend-paying stock has a price of $9.00. The stock trades at $80.00. The call and a European put on the same stock share a strike of $85.00 and a one-year expiry. The annual risk-free rate is 4% (annual compounding). What is the put price, rounded to the nearest cent?
steps: Write parity: $c_0 + X/(1+r)^T = p_0 + S_0$, so $p_0 = c_0 - S_0 + X/(1+r)^T$.
Discount the strike: $85/1.04 = 81.7308$. On the BA II Plus, press 1 [N], 4 [I/Y], 0 [PMT], 85 [FV], then [CPT] [PV] to get -81.73 (ignore the sign).

formulas.name: Put-call parity (European, no income on the underlying)
formulas.where: $c_0$ = European call price today; $p_0$ = European put price today; $S_0$ = spot price of the underlying; $X$ = common strike; $r$ = annual risk-free rate; $T$ = years to expiry.

formulas.name: Put from call
formulas.where: Symbols as above; a synthetic long put is a long call, short stock and a long bond with face $X$.

formulas.name: Call from put
formulas.where: Symbols as above; a synthetic long call is a long put, long stock and borrowing $X/(1+r)^T$.

formulas.name: Payoff of long call plus short put at expiry

exam_traps: Forgetting to discount the strike: using $X$ instead of $X/(1+r)^T$ in the parity equation.
Putting the stock on the wrong side. The stock pairs with the put (protective put), and the bond pairs with the call (fiduciary call).
Applying parity to options with different strikes or expiries, or to American options, where parity is not an exact equality.
Sign errors when rearranging: $p_0 = c_0 - S_0 + PV(X)$, not $c_0 + S_0 - PV(X)$.
Using the wrong discount period, for example not converting a 6-month expiry into years when the rate is annual.

item.stem: An investor holds a European call plus a zero-coupon bond whose face value equals the call's strike and which matures on the expiry date. Which holding in a put and the underlying stock has the same payoff at expiry?

options.text: Buying a put while holding a short position in the stock
options.explanation: Wrong: this flips the sign on the stock. Short stock loses when the price rises, so the payoff is not max(S_T, X).

options.text: A long put combined with a long position in the stock
options.explanation: Correct: the protective put pays max(S_T, X), the same as the fiduciary call (call plus bond with face X).

options.text: A short put combined with a long position in the stock
options.explanation: Wrong: this confuses a protective put with a position that sells the put. The short put adds downside risk instead of a floor.

issues: 2026-10-28: reworded a sentence that borrowed the source's phrasing (copy guard)

item.stem: A European put is priced at $4.00. The underlying stock, which pays no dividends, trades at $50.00. A European call on the same stock has the same $50.00 strike and a one-year expiry. The annual risk-free rate is 4% with annual compounding. Using put-call parity, what is the call price, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: Wrong: the strike is not discounted (4 + 50 - 50), so the time value of money is ignored.
Wrong: this uses p - S + PV(X) = 4 - 50 + 48.08, the put-from-call rearrangement, instead of the call-from-put one.

item.stem: For European options with the same strike and expiry on the same stock, the fiduciary call currently costs more than the protective put. Which action locks in a risk-free profit?

options.text: Buy the fiduciary call and sell the protective put
options.explanation: Wrong: this buys the more expensive portfolio and sells the cheaper one, locking in a certain loss.

options.text: Do nothing, because both portfolios carry market risk
options.explanation: Wrong: both portfolios have identical payoffs, so the risk is the same and the price gap is a pure mispricing.

options.text: Sell the fiduciary call and buy the protective put
options.explanation: Correct: selling the expensive portfolio and buying the cheap one gives a positive cash flow now and exactly offsetting payoffs at expiry.

item.stem: A European call is priced at $7.50. The non-dividend-paying stock trades at $60.00. A European put on the same stock has a $65.00 strike and a one-year expiry, matching the call. The annual risk-free rate is 5% with annual compounding. Using put-call parity, what is the put price, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: Wrong: the strike is not discounted (7.50 - 60 + 65), which ignores the time value of money.
Wrong: the strike is compounded forward (65 x 1.05 = 68.25) instead of discounted back to today.

item.stem: Which combination of positions creates a synthetic long European put?

options.text: Long a call, short the stock, and buy a zero-coupon bond with face value equal to the strike
options.explanation: Correct: rearranging parity gives p = c - S + PV(X), so the put is a long call, short stock and long bond.

options.text: Long a call, long the stock, and borrow the present value of the strike
options.explanation: Wrong: this reverses the stock and bond signs. It is closer to a leveraged long stock position than a put.

options.text: Short a call, short the stock, and lend the present value of the strike
options.explanation: Wrong: the call sign is flipped, so the position has the opposite exposure to the call leg of the synthetic put.

item.stem: Why is put-call parity an exact no-arbitrage relationship for European options but not necessarily for American options?

options.text: American options always cost less than European options, so the equation is shifted by a fixed amount
options.explanation: Wrong: the right to exercise early generally makes American options worth at least as much, not less.

options.text: Parity requires the call and put to have different strikes, which American options cannot have
options.explanation: Wrong: parity requires the same strike for both options. American options can have the same strike.

options.text: Early exercise of an American option can break the equal-payoff link between the two portfolios
options.explanation: Correct: with exercise possible before expiry, the portfolios no longer have identical payoffs on every date, so exact equality need not hold.

item.stem: A European put option with a $42.00 strike and one year to expiry is priced at $2.50. The underlying stock pays no dividends and trades at $40.00. A European call on the same stock has the same $42.00 strike and the same expiry. The annual risk-free rate is 3% with annual compounding. Using put-call parity, what is the call price, rounded to the nearest cent?

options.explanation: Uses the put-from-call rearrangement, p - S + PV(X) = 2.50 - 40.00 + 40.78, with the signs on S and PV(X) flipped. The correct call-from-put form adds the stock price and subtracts the discounted strike.
Correct. Parity gives c = p + S - X/(1+r)^T. The discounted strike is 42/1.03 = 40.7767, so c = 2.50 + 40.00 - 40.7767 = 1.7233, which rounds to $1.72.
Leaves the strike undiscounted (2.50 + 40.00 - 42.00), so it ignores the time value of money. The strike is paid a year from now and must be discounted at the risk-free rate.

item.stem: At expiry, an investor is long a European call and short a European put, both with strike X on the same underlying. The underlying price at expiry is S_T. What is the payoff of this combined position?

options.explanation: Wrong: this is the payoff of a protective put or fiduciary call, not of a long call combined with a short put.
Wrong: this reverses the sign; it is the payoff of a short call combined with a long put.
Correct: if S_T > X the call pays S_T - X; if S_T < X the short put loses X - S_T. Either way the total is S_T - X.

item.front: State put-call parity for European options on a stock paying no income.
item.back: c0 + X/(1+r)^T = p0 + S0, with the same strike X and expiry T for the call and the put.

item.front: What are the two portfolios with identical payoffs in put-call parity?
item.back: Fiduciary call (call + zero-coupon bond with face X) and protective put (put + share). Both pay max(S_T, X) at expiry.

item.front: How do you build a synthetic long put from other instruments?
item.back: Long call + short stock + long zero-coupon bond with face X, since p0 = c0 - S0 + X/(1+r)^T.

item.front: Why does put-call parity hold exactly only for European options?
item.back: American options can be exercised early, so the two portfolios need not have the same payoff at every date.

item.front: If the fiduciary call is priced above the protective put, what is the arbitrage?
item.back: Sell the fiduciary call, buy the protective put, and keep the price difference. The payoffs cancel at expiry.

warnings: 1/7 items have the longest option as the key
